## Summary Enable adaptive min/max filtering of equality-join probe rows through shared machinery used by Parquet, native RLE, and DICT_FSST scans. The design separates two questions: - Does this value pass the filter? Cache that answer. - Is this optional filter saving work? Measure that from actual rows. Required predicates continue to apply when optional filters pause. ## Why this belongs in shared machinery A compressed entry can represent thousands of rows. Counting dictionary entries or runs therefore gives a different picture from counting actual rows. For example, two stored values might each appear once in a dictionary, while one represents almost every row. Evaluating the dictionary can suggest a useful filter even when it rejects almost nothing in practice. Native cached scans have this same problem as Parquet. They can also cache a temporary “accept everything” result when an adaptive filter is paused. Following the review feedback (https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/pull/28515#issuecomment-6821426694), this change replaces the Parquet-specific min/max matcher with shared cache support. ## Implementation The shared implementation provides three guarantees: 1. Pure mask construction. Evaluate the underlying predicate without advancing adaptive counters or recording a paused pass-through result. 2. Feedback from actual row batches. Cached and fallback paths update the same per-filter state. Paused filters still advance their retry clock. 3. Independent mandatory filtering. Keep mandatory and optional results separate, preserving required predicates and evaluation order when optional filters pause. Caches are invalidated when their owning filter state expires. Unsafe predicates, unsupported adaptive expressions, and native segments requiring separate NULL validity use the existing row-evaluation fallback. ## Performance There will be - Before the fix - Original PR with min-max adaptive filter - Then the current after follow comments of reviewer ## The measured tradeoff comparing with original PR Keeping cached answers adds machinery, so we compared it with both the original PR and the simpler row-evaluation fallback. The table below shows earlier selective native-storage fixtures. A millisecond (ms) is one thousandth of a second. Lower times are better. The shared cache was about 36–38% faster than fallback, while costing about 3% for RLE and 6% for the string dictionary versus the original PR. There is a counterexample to a universal speedup: skewed native RLE was 13.7% slower than fallback. These were small warm tests before the upstream merge: 737,280 rows, one thread, 18 measured queries per image and case. Timings were not repeated after that merge. Deprecated change - reference as bellow
Equality-join min/max fallback filters currently prune Parquet row groups - But do not reject individual probe rows when groups overlap the build range. Then - **Enable adaptive row** evaluation and **keep scalar comparisons** on the **fast executor path**. Parquet measures actual row rejection outside dictionary-mask evaluation, keeps cached predicates deterministic, and preserves periodic pause/resume so an unrepresentative prefix cannot disable filtering for the whole group. Predicates proved exactly `ALWAYS_TRUE` skip evaluation. The specialized path accepts direct scalar ranges; other expression shapes use the existing evaluator. Regression coverage includes - Selective filtering within overlapping groups, - Recovery after a matching prefix, - Dictionary row-frequency feedback, - Mandatory predicates, NULL semantics and native scans. Validation: - TDD: the baseline emits 180,000 probe rows for 18,060 join matches. - The selective scan, recovery and dictionary-feedback regressions pass with the implementation. - Saved validation records for the rebased tree show 34 SQL comparisons, 17 native checks, and 183 assertions across five focused sqllogictest files (51 assertions in the three new regression files). These are targeted results, not a full-suite claim. - Scoped formatting and `git diff --check` pass; the optional local spelling tool was unavailable. - [Fork PR and CI results](https://github.com/kevintruong/duckdb/pull/2). T ## Parent-versus-head performance evaluation Re-evaluated - Upstream parent `6145a8699b5e54b146fb305a862012b58130e9b8` - Against PR head `0b6d5a35edeb9c9bd6d76233dffc29ff9a985eb1` - Using matching macOS arm64 compiler flags: `-O3`, assertions enabled, sanitizers disabled. - -The saved head runtime reports pre-amend build ID `7cd49cc31c`; its evaluated source blobs were verified against the final PR head. | Workload | Grounded finding | |---|---| | Selective join | Approximately 65% faster, about 2.9× speedup | | Broad and redundant-broad | Approximately 1.8% more executed instructions | | 90%-match | Instruction count essentially unchanged | | Native broad-match | No consistent slowdown established | The runs use the original issue's - 30-million-row probe fixture - Identical SQL/settings - And paired runtime order. Selective speedup is the paired geometric-mean estimate at two threads: - Head/parent time ratio `0.346` (95% bootstrap interval `0.324–0.370`). - Probe output falls from 30 million to 3.01 million rows while all 245 row groups are still scanned; this is not an I/O reduction claim. Controls use order-entry thresholds of 14 minutes (broad), 2,100 minutes (approximately 90% match), and 18,900 minutes (selective), with redundant probe predicates `ol_o_id >= 2` or `ol_o_id >= 2700`. Timing batches include 8 paired rounds and an independent 12-round confirmation with an identical-head-binary control; native and single-thread controls are also included. All 399 workload executions matched count/SUM checks, including 300 unprofiled timed queries and 24 profiles. Profiled runs did not spill. Instruction measurements are whole-process counts at one thread, with five queries per native process, including startup/setup. - Observed changes were `+1.815%` for broad, - `+1.814%` for redundant-broad, - And `−0.065%` for the 90% control. - - These percentages describe executed work, not wall-clock regressions. Related to #28269. AI-assisted implementation and validation.

AI-assisted review:

> Thanks for the PR! Could we address this through the shared filter machinery? Native `RLEFilter` and `DictFSSTFilter` also evaluate filters over run values/dictionary entries and cache the matches. They therefore have the same mismatch between adaptive feedback and actual row frequency.
>
> A straightforward starting point would be a shared capability indicating whether a filter can safely be evaluated once and cached. Adaptive filters would use the existing row-evaluation fallback in both native and Parquet scans; deterministic filters could retain dictionary/run-mask filtering. This would also handle mixed mandatory and optional predicates without the Parquet-specific min/max expression matcher.
>
> If benchmarks show that retaining cached masks for adaptive filters is worthwhile, the implementation needs these explicit guarantees:
>
> - Mask construction always evaluates the underlying predicate, without advancing adaptive counters or capturing a temporary “paused” result.
> - Adaptive decisions advance on actual row batches, including batches served through cached masks.
> - Pausing an optional predicate still applies mandatory predicates. A combined `mandatory AND optional` mask needs separable results or a fallback.
>
> Please validate skewed row frequencies, a matching prefix followed by a selective tail, and mandatory predicates sharing the filtered column. Include Parquet and persisted native tables with verified RLE/dictionary compression. I would benchmark the simpler fallback before adding another adaptive execution path.

The native row-frequency concern is confirmed: 

- the two-entry sample reports 50% passing and remains active, while six actual row batches report 99.9512% passing and pause. 
- The shared `can_cache` guard now routes adaptive filters through row evaluation in native and Parquet scans, before Parquet's NULL probe; deterministic masks remain. 
- The Parquet-only min/max matcher and external counters are removed.


Including checkpoint/reopen with verified RLE and DICT_FSST encoding, skewed frequencies, prefix/tail recovery, mandatory predicates and NULLs. 

- The broad local selection passed **33,379 assertions in 403 cases** with 18 skips;

- The adaptive SQL tests also pass under warnings-as-errors, optimizer-disabled and serializer-verification configs.

Counts and sums match in all 12 cases. Broad Parquet controls are about 5.5–6.8% slower; mostly matching native cases improve about 6–14%. The selective Parquet variants emit the same number of scan rows, so the slowdown there is not explained by additional admitted rows alone.

> > Two correctness issues need fixing first:

> > 1. **Restore Parquet page-skipping safety.** Removing the NULL-rejection check exposes wrong results for REQUIRED dictionary columns. When a vector crosses a page boundary, the ordinary-read fallback represents skipped rows as NULLs. A NULL-accepting predicate can then return those placeholders. The repro below returns **6,001 rows, all NULL**, instead of zero on this head.
> >    Require proof that NULL cannot pass before using the all-dictionary-values-rejected **page-skipping shortcut**. Establish that fact through pure evaluation, without training adaptive counters or capturing a paused result, and reset it when rebuilding the cache. Keep ordinary dictionary filtering available. Add the required-column/page-boundary regression, with nullable and non-dictionary controls.
> > 2. **Synchronize the segment-statistics read.** [TSan reports a race](https://github.com/duckdb/duckdb/actions/runs/43385964286) between the new `StandardColumnData::Filter` `GetStats().CanHaveNull()` read and `BaseStatistics::Merge` during append finalization. Apply the existing fallback eligibility checks first, then protect any remaining statistics read with the owning `ColumnData::stats_lock`; release it before fallback/filter evaluation. Moving the read alone does not establish safety. Re-run the reported TSan batch.
> > 3. **Keep mixed-run RLE filtering proportional to runs.** The new `RLEFilter` expands one run index per row, applies masks, then gathers values, including for mandatory predicates. Could we apply the cache to run fragments and materialize surviving rows afterwards?
> >    Both feedback and dense-bypass decisions must use fragment **row lengths**, not run counts. Record predicate acceptance before bypass; the next conjunction child receives the selection actually retained. Update each reached optional node once per nonempty logical batch, including recovery while paused. Calling `FilterConstant` once per run would advance the sampler too often. Keep accounting in the shared cache layer and external selections as logical row IDs. Retain the selected-input fallback and constant/accept-all shortcuts. If necessary, preserve the fused pure-mask path for mandatory filters.
> > 4. **Enable pure Bloom/prefix-range child caches.** `BloomFilterExecutor` and `PrefixRangeFilterExecutor` lack `CanCache`/`CreateCache`, forcing even a conjunction containing them onto row evaluation. Inside the selectivity-optional wrapper they already omit their own sampler. Reuse the Boolean cache for that pure case, preserving the existing publication/lifetime contract: the bound filter must be fully published and immutable, not merely `IsInitialized()`. Keep all feedback in the outer optional cache. Preserve NULL handling and fallback for unready filters or children with independent adaptive state.
